stories.body:
Free AI models that are as good as the investment-hungry US versions will disrupt global markets, and offer Britain a lesson

A lmost from the moment it began, the end of the Chinese economic miracle has been much anticipated. Thick and fast, the books have come explaining how it will end badly. Overinvestment. A country wallowing in debt. The collapse of the property market . Political repression. The demand for democracy from a growing middle class. All have been put forward as reasons for the inevitable terminal crisis.

Even those impressed by the country’s rapid growth took comfort from the notion that the west would continue to dominate advanced manufacturing while China would be stuck assembling TVs. And while the wait for its much-predicted demise has gone on and on, China has become the workshop of the world.

This process has come in two distinct phases. Initially, it is true, there was a concentration on low-cost manufactured goods because cheap labour costs provided a competitive advantage. Firms left for east Asia in search of higher profits. Without China 1.0, Donald Trump would have remained a New York property developer and Brexit might never have happened.

Yet, the Chinese were not content to remain solely the producers of low-cost consumer goods and began to invest heavily in higher-end manufacturing. China 2.0 shattered the illusion that it would forever remain a developing economy destined to produce low-grade products and little else.

The market in solar panels was captured. It became the world leader in batteries and electric vehicles . It no longer has to import machine tools from Germany because it is now capable of making its own. The rise of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland is in no small measure due to the threat posed by China to German manufacturing jobs.

Of course, China’s critics have a point. The model relies too heavily on investment and has much excess capacity. The country produces far more goods than it can consume domestically, particularly given the low level of wages and a relatively ungenerous welfare system. As a result, China can only keep growing at a rate that prevents rising unemployment from leading to social unrest if it exports its surfeit of goods to the rest of the world. China found itself isolated at the recent meeting of finance ministers of the G20 group of leading developed and developing countries, facing criticism from all sides for failing to boost domestic demand for its products .

Perhaps this means the rest of the world has finally woken up to the threat. If it has, that would not be a moment too soon because China is now competing with the US for dominance in the race to develop artificial intelligence. Welcome to China 3.0.

In July, a Chinese startup called Moonshot unveiled its Kimi K3 model and it was an instant success. Just two days after its launch, the company suspended new subscriptions because demand was too great for its computing capacity. That was not surprising given that Kimi K3 was marketed as being able to match the models of its US rivals – such as the latest versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT – at no cost. This was not a fluke or a random event.

As Edoardo Campanella of UniCredit notes, Beijing is pursuing a clear AI strategy: staying close to the technological frontier, diffusing its models throughout the global economy, and setting standards across international markets. “If this strategy succeeds, the third China shock might not just disrupt the global economy, but also the global balance of power ,” says Campanella.

Beijing’s strategy might not succeed but even so there are three things that are striking about the AI development race. The first is that this would appear to be the worst possible time for Washington to antagonise its traditional allies by whacking them with punitive tariffs. The US needs all the friends it can muster.

The second is that the arrival on the scene of free Chinese AI models could spell big trouble for global markets. Until now, the US has been confident its technological prowess will give it the upper hand in the AI development race and that has justified massive investment in technology companies.

Despite rising oil prices, share prices on Wall Street have reflected confidence not just that AI will transform economies but that the US will be the main beneficiary. But if China can develop its AI models at a lower cost and offer them for nothing, investors will soon start to question whether the massive investment in the US justifies the sky-high share prices of tech companies. China’s success in AI could prick the stock market bubble .

after newsletter promotion

Finally, there are lessons that countries such as Britain need to learn from China if it is to re-industrialise. When China began to build up its manufacturing strength almost 50 years ago, it saw itself as a developing country. It had no illusions about the scale of the challenge but had a plan and stuck to it.

There was no aversion to picking winners. Nor would the strategy be left exposed to the whims of speculators. Instead, there was a willingness to use all the policy tools available: subsidies, tariffs, exchange controls and state investment.

The result is what we see now: a China that has shifted through the gears from an industrial policy dominated by cheap goods to an industrial policy of everything. Sure, China’s model has its flaws but there is a stark contrast with Britain’s negligent approach since the late 1970s. One country is serious about manufacturing and the other isn’t.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

stories.title: Spending deal comes with a bonus: Blocking political control of grants
stories.summary: Congress pauses the OMB's attempt to rewrite how research is funded.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Congress pauses the OMB’s attempt to rewrite how research is funded.

On Tuesday, the House of Representatives passed a stopgap measure that would continue funding the US government through early December. While the measure still requires the signature of President Trump, it’s widely expected that he will act to avoid a government shutdown immediately before the midterm elections.

This is a normal part of how the US government has operated in recent years, as it’s often difficult to build the political support needed to pass a full year’s budget in advance. In fact, dissent within the House’s Republican caucus prevented them from agreeing on their own measure to keep the government open; instead, the House simply adopted a version of the spending bill that had previously passed the Senate.

From the perspective of scientists and their supporters, that adoption turned out to be a very good thing, because the Senate’s budget bill, passed in early August , contains a provision that blocks the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) from implementing new rules that would give political appointees full control over what science is funded and allow them to cancel any grant at any time. The proposed rule has been widely decried as catastrophic for science, and it faced widespread opposition from scientific and health-focused organizations.

That opposition likely contributed to two senators, Patty Murray (D-Wash.) and Susan Collins (R-Maine), inserting language into the budget deal that prevents the OMB from implementing it prior to the expiration of the stopgap measure on December 11.

While this is not a permanent reprieve, it does signal that the legislature is not interested in handing OMB and other administration officials that much control over federal spending—the bill passed the Senate by a 90-6 margin, and by 370-48 in the House, where opposition largely focused on other aspects of the measure. Those margins raise the prospect that similar language could be inserted into any further budget deals without triggering opposition.

stories.title: Trump $1 coin makes him first living president on US currency in a century
stories.summary: The US Mint special edition is stamped with a portrait of Trump alongside the words "LIBERTY" and "IN GOD WE TRUST"
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 3 September 2026, 02:56 BST

Donald Trump's portrait has made its way on to a US coin - the latest move by the president to put his personal stamp on American institutions.

On Wednesday, the US Mint launched the $1 coin with a portrait of Trump alongside the words "LIBERTY" and "IN GOD WE TRUST", to celebrate America's 250th anniversary.

The Mint said the coins were not being put into circulation, but they may be used as legal tender.

Federal law prohibits a living president from appearing on US currency, but a design clause in legislation for the anniversary was used to overcome the ban.

The coins - priced at $61 (£45) for a roll of 25 and $154.50 for a bag of 100 - were "not currently in stock" on the mint's website within hours of going on sale. They were also being sold in vending machines at the US Mint store in Washington DC.

The BBC has contacted the US Mint, the Treasury and the White House for further details.

The coin has been "created to celebrate this historic national milestone" with a "once-in-a-generation anniversary design destined to become a standout addition to modern collections", the US Mint said.

While the coins have a golden colour they do not contain any actual gold. According to the US Mint, they are 88.5% copper with the balance being made up of zinc, manganese and nickel.

Vending machines selling Trump $1 coins at the US Mint store in Washington DC

In May, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his department was planning to issue a new $250 bill bearing a portrait of President Trump .

At the time, Bessent highlighted that another living US president has previously appeared on the country's currency.

A half-dollar that was issued to commemorate America's 150th anniversary in 1926 featured then-President Calvin Coolidge.

The Trump administration has also cited the Circulating Collectible Coin Redesign Act of 2020, from Trump's first term.

While this statute prohibits portraits of living people on the reverse (tails side) of coins, it does not explicitly cover the obverse (heads side), where Trump's likeness appears on the new $1 coins.

In March, the Treasury announced that US paper money would soon bear Trump's signature - another first for a sitting US president.

stories.body:
About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border

After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts

Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.

Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.

Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.

The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.

At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.

According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.

Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.

Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.

“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal ⁠electricity authority, told Reuters.

Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.

“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”

“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”

Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.

The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet , which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through ‌the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”

At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels ⁠because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we ​are told there is a ​dry space inside. We are ​trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.

The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology ​available in Nepal ‌right now, and we ​are taking help ​from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.

Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.

She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”

She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”

Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.

According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

stories.title: Zack Polanski says he'll run for former PM Starmer's seat in by-election
stories.summary: The Green Party leader intends to run in the Holborn and St Pancras seat following Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as MP.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Zack Polanski has not been an MP in the UK Parliament before

Published 3 September 2026, 09:14 BST

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has confirmed he wants to stand in the by-election brought about by Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as an MP.

Polanski, who is currently a London Assembly member but not a member of Parliament, said he was "so excited by the prospect" of being the first Green MP for Holborn and St Pancras.

The Greens are targeting the seat, until now a Labour stronghold, after coming second to Labour in the area in local elections earlier this year.

Sir Keir announced on Tuesday that he was quitting as MP for the London constituency, two months after he stood down as prime minister, setting up a challenging by-election for his successor Andy Burnham.

In comments to the Camden New Journal , external on Thursday morning, Polanski said: "I have lived and worked in this community over many years, I know it well and I love it.

"It represents so many of the things that make London so special. I am so excited by the prospect of representing this place in Parliament."

He added: "It's a clear fight between Labour and the Green Party."

The Green Party currently has five MPs.

In order to officially be the Green candidate for the seat, Polanski needs to be selected by local party members - something his comments suggest will happen.

But there have been reports in recent days of splits among local Green activists, some of whom are said to favour a Palestinian candidate or a pro-Gaza independent.

Andrew Feinstein, the independent runner-up to Sir Keir in the constituency at the 2024 general election, said he believes Polanski will be an "excellent candidate".

Writing on X, Feinstein said: "Unfortunately I am not in a position to stand this time round."

He said the Camden People's Alliance will meet next week to formally decide its position, adding: "This is a crucial time for progressives in Camden and across the country to be united."

A date has not yet been set for the by-election.

The stakes were already high for Labour at this by-election, because it offers an early test of Burnham's ability to stave off the Green threat in inner-city constituencies.

With Polanski's candidacy, the stakes are even higher for the Greens, to see whether they make good on their leader's oft-stated ambition to replace Labour.

Polanski said a Green victory would be a "clear message that we won't sit by as we get poorer and extreme wealth is concentrated at the very top."

Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP Published 1 day ago

Sir Keir had been MP for the area since 2015, but said he was quitting to focus on a role in international affairs.

The former prime minister had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.

He said it was the "right time" for him to "pass the baton to a successor".

"I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world," he said, adding he would also continue his work combatting violence against women and girls.

Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.

Labour has not decided its candidate to potentially take on Polanski, with applications closing on Friday.

stories.title: Trump may be forced to reveal secret rules feds use for AI safety testing
stories.summary: Trump’s secret reviews of frontier AI models may hide corruption, lawsuit says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Trump’s secret reviews of frontier AI models may hide corruption, lawsuit says.

Four federal agencies have been sued amid calls to release information about the secret framework that the Trump administration uses to conduct safety reviews of frontier AI models prior to release.

In a Wednesday press release announcing the lawsuit, a nonpartisan nonprofit called Protect Democracy alleged that “almost no details” have been released to the public or Congress. To everyone except a few vague “trusted partners,” it remains unclear what the government’s review process looks like, which companies are involved in constructing the framework, or what legal authority Trump officials have to conduct the reviews.

“Neither the identities of those entities nor the criteria by which they were selected have been made public,” Protect Democracy said.

That’s a problem, Protect Democracy alleged in a statement to Ars, since decisions about “which AI models are approved and released may be the most important policy question of this White House.” And it appears that at least one AI firm, OpenAI, has “negotiated a private agreement with the Federal Government to limit distribution of its cutting-edge AI models to government-vetted partners.”

The group’s lawsuit is seeking an order requiring officials to produce all information sought by September 30. That includes “unclassified procedural and contractual architecture: the framework’s text, the terms of participation, the identity of participants, and the process and criteria by which access to frontier models is granted or withheld,” the complaint said. They also want an injunction restraining officials from improperly withholding records that aren’t classified.

“The executive branch is now choosing which companies can release their products and which customers get access to a technology that could shape the future of not only American industry and national security, but economies and governments abroad as well,” Protect Democracy’s release said. “All with no oversight from Congress, the public, or tech experts outside of the executive branch.”

Secret rules allegedly hide corruption

According to Protect Democracy, the framework could potentially be “corrupt,” with officials from the Office of the National Cyber Director, the Office of Science and Technology Policy, the Treasury Department, and the Commerce Department potentially favoring rapid deployments for AI firms that Trump likes. And on the flip side, the public has already seen Trump retaliate against an AI firm for being too woke, Protect Democracy noted, pointing to a judge’s recent ruling that it was illegal for Trump to blacklist Anthropic .

As AI technology advances and cybersecurity risks escalate— OpenAI’s model hacking Hugging Face is the most obvious recent example—the public can’t afford to blindly trust Trump to act in good faith when choosing which frontier models should be rigorously tested, Protect Democracy said. And perhaps even worse, the public cannot know if new vulnerabilities discovered in the real world are due to agencies failing to complete a proper review, running outdated or ineffective tests, missing important checks, or missing steps that align with the latest mitigation strategies advanced by leading AI safety experts.

“We deserve to know what’s in the framework,” the group said, joining other calls for the agencies to be more transparent about AI model deployments.

In a post on X last month, US Representative Greg Casar (D-Tx.) accused Trump of “completely failing to keep us safe from the dangers of AI” while taking “millions from AI billionaires.”

“Now, in the wake of extremely dangerous AI cybersecurity problems, he says he’s set up ‘voluntary’ review that no one has seen,” Casar said. “Asleep at the wheel. Too busy cashing in to protect our jobs or national security.”

More recently, another Democrat, California state Senator Josh Becker, urged the court to grant Protect Democracy’s request. In a declaration supporting their complaint, Becker noted that California is mulling a bill, SB 813 , that would establish a process where independent organizations would set baselines for AI safety standards. If passed—unlike Trump’s approach—California’s plan would make the latest benchmarks, standards, and methodologies used to evaluate risks posed by AI systems transparent to the public, Becker said. Already, public input has shaped the bill, he noted, with one provision withdrawn following public backlash.

“In contrast to the Administration’s approach, every step of SB 813’s development has been public,” Becker wrote, emphasizing that “we are accountable for the framework we have set.”

No one knows Trump’s “trusted partners”

The Trump administration has been rushing to set up the voluntary safety review process ever since the government flagged Anthropic’s Mythos 5 model as too dangerous to release earlier this summer. The plan was to rapidly expand industry collaborations so that government teams at the Center for AI Standards and Innovation could review prerelease models with reduced or removed safeguards to “thoroughly evaluate national security-related capabilities and risks.” But that would be impossible, Trump realized, without industry experts being fully transparent and explaining what exactly new models could do.

In July, the White House launched a clearinghouse, GOLD EAGLE , that relies on industry partners to help agencies flag cybersecurity vulnerabilities across many sectors and industries. Again, Protect Democracy noted that the “White House did not identify any company participating in GOLD EAGLE, the terms on which they are participating, or any legal authority for the program.”

Then, on August 3, the White House announced that it had completed the voluntary framework for reviewing AI models before their public release. Both the framework and GOLD EAGLE are actively being used to review frontier models as the technology advances, the White House has confirmed.

Some parts of the government’s review process are classified. The executive order explained that Trump planned to develop “a classified benchmarking process” that would assess advanced capabilities of AI models and determine when models should be designated as frontier AI.

However, Protect Democracy’s complaint said the framework itself is notably not designated as classified. Despite that, the White House has refused to share details with the public. Instead, a spokesperson told reporters that “just because things are unclassified, that doesn’t mean we are going to broadcast them to everyone.”

Additionally concerning, the term “covered frontier model” is not defined, Protect Democracy said. If the definition is too narrow, some dangerous AI models could slip through the cracks, and if it’s too broad, agencies recently gutted by DOGE cuts may be spread too thin to assess too many models at once. Without more clarity, the public “can only hope this powerful technology is being governed safely and in the public interest,” Protect Democracy alleged.

So far, the framework has only been shared with “a select set of AI companies,” which excludes meaningful stakeholders, such as AI safety groups currently warning of emerging societal risks, as well as smaller or emerging AI firms whose input or model reviews may be just as critical.

Protect Democracy regularly relies on making FOIA requests in its mission to “prevent American democracy from declining into a more authoritarian form of government,” the complaint said. Fearing that Trump was seizing too much power over AI, the group sent identical FOIA requests to four US agencies, urgently seeking only non-classified information and requesting that their request be expedited. So far, no agency has produced any records, the complaint said. Only the National Cyber Director’s office responded, but it denied the group’s request to expedite the process, which Protect Democracy is now challenging as improper.

Congress is in the dark, too

On top of leaving the public in the dark—and independent researchers, advocacy groups, AI investors, and businesses in many industries with a stake in AI—lawmakers have been blocked from assessing the executive branch’s AI safety framework.

That matters, Protect Democracy alleged, because Trump’s AI safety operation may be destabilized if Congress is not on the same page. Right now, Congress is mulling whether to renew the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act (CISA) of 2015, which seemingly is the sole legal basis allowing AI firms to share information with the government through GOLD EAGLE, the complaint said.

Those protections are part of a CISA provision that lapsed once, and Congress must soon decide if the provision should be extended. There’s discord between the House of Representatives and the Senate on the deadline to vote on the extension, but the earliest that could happen is September 30 and the latest is December 11.

“In either event, Congress will soon need to decide whether to extend CISA’s liability protections that, by the administration’s own account, sustain the GOLD EAGLE program that the administration has announced but has yet to explain,” Protect Democracy’s complaint said. “Indeed, a senior administration official publicly acknowledged at GOLD EAGLE’s launch that, absent that reauthorization, ‘this effort is fundamentally challenged.’”

Deana El-Mallawany, director of Impact Programs & Counsel at Protect Democracy, told Ars that “neither Protect Democracy nor Congress has enough information about the GOLD EAGLE program to make a fully informed decision on extending CISA. Our concern is that the White House is putting Congress in the position of voting on a CISA extension without knowing how the GOLD EAGLE program is operating, who’s involved, or what statutory authority is being invoked. That’s why we’re seeking these records.”

Protect Democracy alleged that without these records, the Trump administration could escape accountability for AI safety review.

“Congress cannot meaningfully oversee programs whose terms and asserted authority it has not been shown” and “courts cannot review action they cannot identify,” the complaint said.

El-Mallawany told Ars that if Protect Democracy gets access to the framework, all documents will be posted publicly. Without more transparency, the list of concerns that Protect Democracy has about Trump’s potential ability to leverage the voluntary framework over the AI industry is long , El-Mallawany said, adding:

The risks are abundant, including the risk that the White House could use the secret process to coerce AI companies over decisions like whether to deploy AI for lethal autonomous weapons and mass surveillance (as we saw with the clash between the Pentagon and Anthropic), to extort certain investors and employees for political and financial support or punish others for perceived political opposition, or to force AI companies to incorporate politicized viewpoints into their models—not to mention the risk that the review framework is simply ineffective, creating a false sense of security.

stories.title: Taiwan’s six-year hunt for China’s undercover chip labs
stories.summary: Previously unpublished government data reveals the scale of Taiwan’s crackdown on Chinese companies accused of hiding their ties while recruiting chip talent and pursuing sensitive technology.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Features

Previously unpublished government data reveals the scale of Taiwan’s crackdown on Chinese companies accused of hiding their ties while recruiting chip talent and pursuing sensitive technology.

I n the spring of 2020, a Taiwanese engineer felt “extremely lucky” to be offered a job as a chip designer at Blue Ocean Smart System, an American company based in his hometown Hsinchu, the heart of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. He said the role gave him a chance to work on an ambitious AI-chip design project and a $120,000 salary, doubling the industry average, which would help pay off his two children’s private elementary education.

But several months into his new role, the engineer, who was 32 at the time, noticed something strange: He was never in touch with any American coworkers, and there was no information about the U.S. office. Instead, he told Rest of World , he spent most of his time working with team members based in Nanjing, China. That’s who he spoke with in weekly online meetings, and with whom he shared his engineering code and chip designs.

What followed confirmed the engineer’s suspicion: In August 2021, Taiwanese authorities raided Blue Ocean Smart System , alleging that the company illegally operated in Taiwan by disguising its Chinese ownership behind a locally registered company.

The Taiwan-registered company shared the exact same English name as Nanjing-based Blue Ocean Smart System, while its Chinese name differed by just one character. The Taiwan operation was later forced to shut down. Blue Ocean Smart System in Nanjing did not respond to Rest of World ’s requests for comment.

“I was explicitly told that the company was backed by American investment,” the engineer told Rest of World , recalling the inconsistencies he picked up during his time there. “But I kept going because I was happy at my job.”

Blue Ocean Smart System is one of the 166 cases investigated by Taiwanese authorities over the past six years for allegedly concealing ties to China, according to exclusive data provided to Rest of World by Taiwan’s Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau, or MJIB. Another 67 China-related trade-secret probes in the technology sector were completed in the same period, according to MJIB figures that have not previously been made public.

The crackdown remains active. As recently as August 5, the MJIB announced it had raided another 18 technology companies, following operations carried out just days earlier between July 13 and August 4.

Taiwan is a global powerhouse in chip manufacturing. Thanks to companies like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company — known as TSMC — Mediatek, and United Microelectronics Corporation, the island nation produces over 60% of the world’s semiconductors and 90% of the world’s most advanced chips. But the strength and vibrancy of the industry has also attracted unwanted interference, with Chinese competitors accused of illegal investments and talent poaching. Taiwan’s crackdown reflects a broader trend to limit China’s access to critical technology across the world, and in the U.S.

Almost everyone in the industry would know or have heard of people who were approached or worked for Chinese companies.” John Chen, a board director at Taiwan-listed chip design company MicroIP

In Taiwan, Chinese investments are scrutinized by a unique legal framework due to the political tensions between the two governments. Under the Cross-Strait Act and related investment regulations, Chinese companies — whether they’re a bubble tea shop or a tech company — are required to obtain government approval before operating on the self-ruled island.

Chinese companies have repeatedly skirted these regulations by operating outside official approval, setting up shell companies, or registering their operations under non-Chinese nationals.

Semicon Taiwan, Asia’s biggest semiconductor trade event, is held in Taiwan each September. Last year, over 100,000 industry professionals from 65 countries attended. Sam Yeh/AFP via Getty Images

Tai Yuen Hi-Tech Industrial Park in Hsinchu is home to approximately 300 companies. Lam Yik Fei for Rest of World

In 2020, Taiwan stepped up enforcement amid intensifying concerns over China’s tech industry from both Taiwanese and U.S. authorities. MJIB, the island’s equivalent of the FBI, kicked off a special operation involving all of its 2,000 investigators to look into Chinese-linked investments in its technology sector.

China has criticized these investigations as “political manipulation.” In 2022, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office spokesperson at the time, Ma Xiaoguang, accused Taiwan’s ruling party of “smearing and intimidating mainland enterprises in Taiwan” with raids that were “politically motivated attempts to obstruct” cooperation and would ultimately harm business interests.

Meanwhile, Taiwanese authorities say this Chinese business activity represents a risk to national security. This past April, Taiwan’s National Security Bureau published a report warning that China continues to use “indirect channels” for “talent poaching, technology theft, and the acquisition of controlled goods” to obtain advanced chipmaking technologies in order to “break through international technological containment.”

“Almost everyone in the industry would know or have heard of people who were approached or worked for Chinese companies,” John Chen, a board director at Taiwan-listed chip design company MicroIP, told Rest of World . “Salary offers often involve five times that in Taiwan. … I have heard it later even went up to 10 times. There are a few friends I know who went to China to work because of that,” said Chen, who has spent nearly four decades in the semiconductor industry. Rest of World ’s review of court filings, combined with interviews with Taiwanese semiconductor engineers, lawyers, and industry insiders, illustrate the efforts Chinese companies have taken to tap Taiwan’s chip sector — and the work that the Taiwanese government has done to fight them off. The Tai Yuen Hi-Tech Industrial Park is made up of 21 office buildings arranged along wide streets on the outskirts of Taiwan’s semiconductor capital Hsinchu. On a weekday afternoon this spring, the sprawling complex, which houses 300 different tech companies, felt quiet and industrious, with only a handful of employees lingering outside a nearby 7-Eleven. The first major raid in the park came in May 2021, less than a year after the MJIB launched the targeted operations. The investigation targeted a Taiwan-registered company tied to the Chinese networking equipment maker Gongjin Electronics. Gongjin initially attempted to register officially with the Taiwanese government, but the registration was rejected by authorities, who alleged that the company had ties to the Chinese military. Subsequently, prosecutors said, Gongjin set up a Taiwan-registered company using a foreign investment structure, listing a Japanese national as its registered representative — although the operational funds still came from China. Registering as a non-Chinese foreign entity or as a foreign person to disguise Chinese affiliations is one of the most common tactics used by Chinese tech companies to hire Taiwanese engineers, Cheng Lun Huang, a senior supervising prosecutor and spokesperson for the Hsinchu District Prosecutors Office, told Rest of World . Cheng Lun Huang, a senior supervising prosecutor for the Hsinchu district, said cases involving Chinese investment in the tech industry are given extra attention. Lam Yik Fei for Rest of World Taiwan has strengthened protection of its semiconductor industry in recent years. In 2022, it tightened the Cross-Strait Act and National Security Act with harsher recommended punishments for offenses. The tougher laws were introduced to protect “critical technologies” and Taiwan’s economic competitiveness, amid a growing number of cases involving Chinese companies’ illegal activities on the island, according to an evaluation report for a legislative proposal passed into law in May that year. The legislative changes came as Beijing accelerated its drive for semiconductor self-reliance. Since unveiling its “ Made in China 2025 ” strategy in 2015, Beijing has poured billions of dollars into building a domestic chip industry through state funding and industrial policies to hit its goal of producing 70% of its chip usage domestically. China’s efforts ramped up even further after Washington restricted Huawei’s access to advanced chips in 2019, followed by sweeping export controls in the years that followed. According to an affiliate of the China Semiconductor Industry Association, the number of Chinese chip design companies grew from 736 in 2015 to 3,901 by 2025. 166 Technology cases investigated by Taiwanese authorities over the past six years for allegedly concealing ties to China. For Taiwan, protecting its semiconductor expertise specifically from Chinese companies has become central to its broader national security strategy as Beijing has intensified military and political pressure and reiterated its goal of “reunification.” This strategy, often referred to as the “silicon shield,” posits that as long as Taiwan remains a critical node for high-end chip manufacturing, the U.S. and its allies would assist in its defense in case of a Chinese attack. Over the past six years, the Hsinchu District Prosecutors Office has been on the frontline of this strategy. The office charged around 60 cases involving nearly 190 individuals claiming illegal business operations, more than any other prosecutor’s office in Taiwan. The industries under review ranged from chip design and semiconductor equipment to AI servers and advanced computing. Huang said cases involving Chinese investment in the tech industry are given extra attention. “We believe foreign investors are watching closely on how well we can protect our intellectual property,” Huang said. MJIB told Rest of World a total of 166 cases alleging illegal Chinese operations and talent poaching have been completed, and that more investigations are ongoing. MJIB declined to provide further details about its operations. However, Rest of World reviewed public court records for 36 of those investigations through Taiwan’s judicial database. All 36 led to convictions for breaching the Cross-Strait Act by operating tech businesses without approval. Thirty-three of these cases focused on companies doing R&D or chip design. The number does not represent all cases that were prosecuted, since there is no public record of cases until judgments are handed down. MJIB told Rest of World it also investigated 67 China-related trade-secret cases in the technology sector over the past six years. When investigations involve allegations more serious than unauthorized business operations, prosecutors may pursue charges under Taiwan’s National Security Act, which criminalizes the theft or unauthorized transfer of “critical technologies,” and carries penalties of up to 12 years in prison and fines of up to 100 million New Taiwan dollars (about $3.1 million). Over the past five years, the Hsinchu District Prosecutors Office has charged around 60 cases involving nearly 190 individuals claiming illegal business operations, more than any other prosecutor’s office in Taiwan. Lam Yik Fei for Rest of World “Whether a company has obtained the required approvals is usually pretty clear,” Hsinchu’s prosecutor Huang told Rest of World . “The threshold for proving a trade secrets violation is much higher,” he said. About 70% of cases involving illegal Chinese operations result in prosecution by his office, Huang said, compared with roughly 20% of trade-secret theft cases. One of the highest-profile cases involved Xiaomi i Xiaomi Xiaomi is a Chinese consumer electronics company that leads the country in smartphone manufacturing and sales. READ MORE , which Taiwanese authorities alleged was behind an unauthorized smartphone chip R&D operation on the island. While the Chinese consumer electronics giant was legally authorized to sell its products in Taiwan, prosecutors said a Xiaomi co-founder directed two former Xiaomi executives to establish a separate chip development business on the island in 2019. They recruited more than two dozen local engineers. According to court documents, Xiaomi’s Beijing subsidiary paid for the research and compensation costs at the Taiwanese operation. In 2024, the two executives — including a former chief financial officer of Beijing-based Xiaomi — were convicted of illegal business operations under the Cross-Strait Act. Xiaomi has not publicly responded to the allegations. A more recent case involved Chinese smartphone brand OnePlus. A court document last November revealed that Taiwanese authorities had issued an arrest warrant for founder Pete Lau, alleging he was involved in operating an unauthorized software R&D outfit on the island that recruited more than 70 engineers in Taiwan. Prosecutors also charged two Taiwanese citizens with allegedly running the operation on Lau’s behalf since 2014. Lau, who is also the senior vice president and chief product officer at OnePlus’ mother company Oppo, did not respond to Rest of World ’s requests for comment. Neither company responded to requests for comment. It has been very challenging for some of my clients to prove they had no awareness, or had no way to verify, whether their investors’ roots were Chinese.” Vincent Huang, an attorney at the Taipei-based WHP law firm MJIB claims that even major Chinese semiconductor firms such as the Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation, or SMIC, China’s most advanced chip foundry, have used a foreign entity to set up a company in Taiwan to poach tech talent. MJIB’s official press release said that SMIC registered as a Samoan company to operate within Taiwan. Few of the Chinese companies linked to these investigations have publicly responded to the allegations. Gongjin Electronics, Xiaomi, and SMIC did not respond to Rest of World ’s requests for comment. Shanghai-listed chip design company VeriSilicon is one of the few Chinese companies to have publicly commented on legal proceedings against it in Taiwan. After Taiwanese authorities raided the company’s Taiwan subsidiary in 2022 over allegations that it had conducted business activities on the island without the required approval, founder and CEO Wayne Dai, in an interview with Chinese media, said the office was merely for sales activities and had never employed engineers or operated chip-testing equipment. VeriSilicon also did not respond to Rest of World ’s questions. As early as 2014, China had a strong incentive to seek overseas technology and talent as its semiconductor industry tried to play “catch up” with global competitors, Hui He, who heads global tech advisory firm Omdia’s semiconductor research in China, told Rest of World . She said many Chinese companies established operations and hired local talent in places such as Taiwan, South Korea, and the U.S. to advance their products while supporting overseas markets. “These moves were largely driven by business needs,” said He. “They were all abiding by market principles. I don’t think they were driven by geopolitical considerations — it is just how the designated location’s legal system interprets these activities,” she said. “Many Western and Taiwanese semiconductor companies are also still operating in China and hiring locals, isn’t it?” Since MJIB started its investigation six years ago, China has made meaningful progress in certain areas of chip design. But in the most cutting-edge chip technology, experts estimate China still lags behind TSMC by anywhere from three to 10 years . Taiwan produces over 60% of the world’s semiconductors. TSMC While Chinese companies still seek expertise to build advanced technology, He said their reliance on poaching foreign talent has diminished in the last three to five years. “There have been more legal restrictions from places like the U.S. and Taiwan,” she said. “China’s semiconductor industry started to have its own talent pool in the last two years, too.” According to available data , it appears that MJIB’s efforts peaked in 2021, the first full year of its campaign, when it raided 100 companies. But authorities have not released sufficient data to determine whether the decline reflects fewer violations or less investigative activity. Taiwan’s industry insiders and legal experts say there is greater general scrutiny and awareness now of China’s involvement in Taiwan’s tech scene than when the MJIB started its targeted crackdown. Vincent Huang, an attorney at the Taipei-based WHP law firm, told Rest of World he has represented more than a dozen clients summoned for questioning by the MJIB in its investigations into illegal Chinese investment. “It has been very challenging for some of my clients to prove they had no awareness, or had no way to verify, whether their investors’ roots were Chinese,” the attorney told Rest of World. “But now, the Taiwanese public is more aware that working for a company backed by Chinese investments could be illegal,” he said . Beyond Taiwan, countries in other regions have also become increasingly alert to Chinese firms’ efforts to acquire critical technologies. The Netherlands, for example, is investigating the national-security implications of the Chinese ownership of Nexperia , a Dutch semiconductor manufacturer which became controlled by Chinese investors through acquisitions. The Dutch and the Chinese governments have been dealing with this issue through diplomatic channels. In the U.S., authorities have prosecuted cases involving Chinese efforts to obtain critical technology, including trade-secret theft by employees at U.S. aerospace technology companies. In January, a former Google engineer was found guilty in a California court for stealing AI trade secrets for a company he founded in China. Nicholas Eftimiades, a former U.S. defense department official whose work included tracking China’s economic espionage, told Rest of World that Chinese companies tailor their approaches to local conditions. In South Korea, for example, Chinese company recruiters would stand outside tech offices to approach exiting workers, he recounted. Eftimiades, who is now a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank, said he believes that the Chinese companies’ methods targeted by the Taiwanese authorities have largely gone unnoticed by the global community. “The technique appears to be … more specific to Taiwan, at least as far as semiconductors go,” he said. “I think the U.S. has got its hands full trying to wrestle with the theft that happens within its own borders.” However, Eftimiades said the U.S. should not take Chinese activities inside Taiwan lightly, even if most of the allegations are not classified under trade-espionage laws. “It has consequences,” he said. “The problem is we lose trillions of dollars in wealth.” MJIB has investigated 166 companies allegedly involved in illegal Chinese business operations in Taiwan since 2020. MJIB “Is it espionage if I sit there poaching talents? Well, in some places it is. We are dealing with different definitions depending on the country, and it’s a problem,” he said, adding that the U.S. should have a coordinated policy with allies like Taiwan. “If the one thing China has proven, it is flexible and resilient. The minute you step on it one way, they turn around and do another,” he said. For some Taiwanese engineers, the fight against talent poaching by Chinese tech companies has become personal. The Hsinchu-based chip designer, who found himself unwittingly working for a Chinese company, said that after leaving Blue Ocean Smart System, he was approached about joining another small chip-design company. He couldn’t find much information about the company and suspected it was another front for a Chinese operation. He didn’t pursue the position. “I made up my mind to not join startups or companies that risk falling into a gray area involving Chinese investments,” he said. Eventually, he got an offer from an American chip design company. This time, he did his due diligence before taking the job. Watch: Andy Burnham and Emmanuel Macron shake hands outside No 10

Published 3 September 2026, 12:24 BST

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has praised the UK-EU relationship as he holds talks with French President Emmanuel Macron about issues such as small boat crossings in the English Channel and defence.

The pair shook hands and posed for photographs alongside their wives outside 10 Downing Street on Thursday morning.

They are discussing "shared challenges" including the rise of "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally, which the Conservatives say shows the UK government has failed to "smash the gangs".

Burnham said it was "so fitting" that Macron was his first overseas visitor in Downing Street since becoming PM in July, describing him as "our nearest neighbour and close friend Emmanuel".

Macron and Burnham are holding bilateral talks on a range of issues

"It shows what collaboration can achieve, just as we are also showing on Ukraine, on small boats, and also on strengthening the UK-EU relationship. So I look forward to discussing those themes further with you today," Burnham added.

Macron's visit to the UK was primarily to mark the Bayeux Tapestry's loan to the British Museum . The French leader met King Charles at the museum on Wednesday, ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display next week.

In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron are discussing not just small boats but also the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as defence and EU co-operation.

But the "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally - first seen earlier in August with a 15-metre long vessel carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK - are arguably the most pressing challenge facing the pair.

It follows a summer when the overall number of small boat arrivals in the UK fell to a seven-year low.

Between 1 January and 1 September 2026, a total of 16,513 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 2 September 2025 to 1 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier . At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.

Earlier on Tuesday, Home Office Minister Anna Turley said the officers were "just part of the armoury" of more than 1,000 officers on northern French beaches who are now doing "actual intervention" in the water.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that videos in recent weeks "show them going to the boats, slashing them, pushing people back, being bombarded with stones and bricks and coming under a lot of challenge to do that, so they are intervening".

In a post on X , external , in which he said he was "do[ing] politics differently", Burnham laid out the latest small boat, returns and asylum hotel figures, describing smuggling gangs as a "shared European challenge".

Asked about the extra police on French beaches, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC she welcomed European collaboration "but the boats aren't stopping".

"We have spent hundreds of millions, if not billions, paying the French to man the borders," she said.

stories.title: Texas and Florida Step Back from ALPRs
stories.summary: Within the last few days, two important state actions have dealt a big blow to automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks. This is just the latest proof of the growing tide of public opposition to mass surveillance. After years of successful grassroots battles to pull these cameras from local streets, bipartisan momentum is sweeping the country. On August 28, Texas Governor Greg Abbott banned state agencies from spending public funds on Flock cameras . The order dropped just as The Texas Tribune prepared to publish an investigation revealing that a state agency had quietly funneled at least $30 million into building a sprawling surveillance network. Then on August 31, the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) issued a memo , announced by Governor Ron DeSantis, ordering the removal of all ALPRs from the right-of-way on state highways within 30 days. The order revokes all previously approved permits to install ALPRs, and bars transportation officials from issuing future permits. FDOT officials stated that “the recent exponential increase in deployments along our roadways, coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes merit immediate action to preserve Floridians’ sovereignty and quality of life.” FDOT’s action has been followed by a surge of local governments in Florida canceling or pausing their vendor contracts . Much more work remains. Many ALPRs in Florida are not on state highways, but sit on city streets, county roads, residential driveways, and shopping center parking lots—and FDOT's order doesn't touch any of them. Likewise, the Texas directive leaves local agencies free to use city, county, federal, and private funds to install cameras. This week’s good news follows years of pushback from local advocates that has seen dozens of cities sever ties with surveillance companies. According to some metrics , during the last 30 days, an average of three localities per day has halted contracts with Flock. Other advocates have been resisting ALPRs in statehouses and court houses , and by blowing the whistle with investigative activism. The moves in Florida and Texas also illustrate the power that the executive branch can wield to curtail mass surveillance with almost immediate results. stories.title: Judge Rules DOD Unlawfully Retaliated Against Anthropic
stories.summary: A federal judge has sided with Anthropic on its claims that the Department of Defense illegally retaliated against Anthropic’s protected speech by labeling the AI company a “supply chain risk.” The judge found that designation, intended to penalize Anthropic for telling the U.S. military it would not allow their technology to be used for mass surveillance of U.S. persons, “constituted unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment.” EFF joined a coalition of organizations in filing multiple amicus briefs ( here , here ) arguing that the Pentagon had trampled on Anthropics First Amendment rights. We agree with the court’s decision and applaud the judge for slapping down such an obvious act of illegal and unconstitutional retribution by the Pentagon—even as the court left open the broader question of whether a company’s choices about how its technology may be used are protected speech in their own right. From the start of this conflict, EFF argued that companies should not be penalized for not wanting to conduct mass surveillance of US persons. Nor do we want to live in a legal system where our susceptibility to surveillance is hashed out and decided in closed-door contract negotiations between a few powerful people at the military and an AI company. Unfortunately, this ruling does little to address the bigger problem: that Congress has abdicated its responsibility to adopt statutory safeguards to protect our privacy, and instead left us reliant on the whims of private companies to decide when they are and are not willing to help the government conduct mass surveillance. In February 2026, the government began threatening to penalize Anthropic unless it backed off its position that it did not want the U.S. military using its AI product Claude for mass surveillance of Americans or to power autonomous weapons systems. stories.title: ‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged world
stories.summary: As FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feet Since 2020’s Demon’s Souls, Japanese video game director Hidetaka Miyazaki has shown the world a different way to think about game design. His games defy convention with punishing fights, obscure rules, and unknowable, inhospitable worlds. The “Soulslike” genre – named after Demon’s Souls and its sequel Dark Souls – is now ubiquitous, influencing multimillion-sellers from God of War and Star Wars: Jedi to Hollow Knight. Miyazaki’s most recent success, 2022’s Elden Ring , which credited Game of Thrones author George RR Martin as a co-creator, sold over 30m copies and inspired Alex Garland to adapt it for the big screen at A24. It earned Miyazaki a spot on Time magazine’s “most influential” list, an accolade he shares with just one other game developer: Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto. Miyazaki is now 51 and has been FromSoftware’s president since 2014, elevated from game designer to CEO after the success of the Souls series. He has a cherubic face that could pass for 35. He rarely speaks publicly, and never on camera. When he does speak, he answers questions like one of his characters – softly, sadly, his head bowed, making eye-contact only when I am speaking. Outside the studio where we speak is the sprawl of Tokyo’s Shinjuku, an ever-changing maze where tourists get lost and pop-up stores appear and vanish without a trace. Today, a J-pop band performs in the square as the cicadas scream from the trees. A gilded statue of Melania, one of Elden Ring’s toughest bosses, looms over this dimly lit conference room inside From’s headquarters, a bonfire checkpoint away from the chaos. Continue reading...

stories.body:
The Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last election

T o outlast a prime minister always counts as some kind of achievement for an opposition leader, although Kemi Badenoch cannot claim credit for Sir Keir Starmer’s downfall . Sir Keir’s wounds were mostly self-inflicted. To the extent that opposition pressure was involved, it was electoral threats from Reform UK and the Green party that stoked Labour party frustration to a regicidal pitch. The Tory leader’s role was largely as a spectator.

Mrs Badenoch still hopes to use regime change to her advantage. She thinks the economy, and fiscal discipline in particular, will be her most fruitful line of attack. In their first confrontation at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, the Conservative leader called Mr Burnham a “spendthrift” and “people pleaser” who will dodge the tough decisions required to prove Britain’s creditworthiness on international markets. She expects him to yield to Labour MPs’ demands for budget increases, which will then have to be financed with tax rises.

In that scenario, Mrs Badenoch imagines a vacancy for a rehabilitated small-state Conservative party offering hard-headed budget management, less profligate than Labour; more sober and respectable than Reform UK. That message would unite what remains of her depleted party. She can’t compete with Nigel Farage on the terrain of anti-immigrant rhetoric (although that doesn’t stop her aping his stances ). She shows no interest in finding political accommodation for socially liberal, pro-European one-nation Tories who now have more in common with the Liberal Democrats than the modern Conservative party.

This leaves the Tories with a narrow focus on tax cuts, reining in welfare spending and deregulation as a spur to enterprise. Mr Farage supports those things too, but Mrs Badenoch believes that Reform UK’s maverick style and the whiff of impropriety around its financial dealings make it an unreliable vehicle for a classically Thatcherite agenda that belongs, by rights, to Lady Thatcher’s own party.

The claim to be the true keeper of the Thatcherite flame has become a ritual for Tory leaders. The mantle has passed through so many hands, it is threadbare as a political definition in 2026. It was worn most preposterously by Liz Truss, who posted photos of herself on social media recreating iconic images of the Iron Lady in her pomp. She then detonated her government with a “ mini-budget ” that was a crass pastiche of the economic ideas she claimed to venerate – a wild foray into fiscal irresponsibility masquerading as free-market radicalism.

One of the Treasury ministers who enthusiastically endorsed Ms Truss’s plan, Andrew Griffith, was this week appointed Mrs Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor. He replaces Mel Stride, a lower-octane performer who was deemed not to have made sufficient impact in the role. It is a revealing choice that undermines the Tory leader’s plan to make economic competence the centrepiece of her pitch to lead the nation. When considering a potential chancellor, she clearly values the ability to grab attention over economic judgment.

This is consistent with a pattern of failure to engage with the full spectrum of failures over many years that accounts for the scale of Tory defeat at the last election. What Mrs Badenoch imagines to be a political strategy looks more like retreat to an ideological comfort zone in the hope that a second prime minister will self-destruct while she watches from the sidelines.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Bank says gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily and the move will allow it to respond more rapidly in a ‘crisis situation’

The Dutch central bank says it has moved 86 tonnes of its gold reserves out of the US and Canada to London, citing “increasing geopolitical unrest”.

De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) said gold reserves held in London could be traded more easily than those held in New York and Ottawa.

“This makes it the quickest for DNB to deploy in a crisis situation,” the bank said in a statement on Wednesday.

“With this step, we have improved the deployability of the gold reserves. We assume that we will never need to deploy the gold, but it is nevertheless necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” said DNB’s president, Olaf Sleijpen.

The total Dutch gold stock amounted to 612.4 tonnes and was valued at €72.2bn ($83.7bn) at the end of 2025, said the DNB.

Before the deployment, the Dutch bank held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa.

After the move, each country accounted for 18.5% of the Dutch gold reserve.

The share of gold held in London increased from 18.1% to 32.1%. The bank still holds 30.8% of its gold in the Netherlands .

The transfer was carried out partially by buying and selling and partly by physically transferring gold, the bank said.

The bank moved more than 27 tonnes of physical gold from the US and Canada to Zeist.

The same quantity of gold was moved from Zeist to London, preventing the melting down of gold bars.

“By combining buying and selling and physical transport, the risks associated with physically moving a large quantity of gold have been spread,” the DNB said.

The operation took place between March and August of this year, it said.

Laurent Schwartz, president of the Paris-based National Gold Counter, which facilitates gold trading in France, said central banks had been moving their reserves around for about a decade.

“The current political context in the United States might also push certain central banks into favouring other storage locations,” he said.

The London market was the deepest and most liquid, Schwartz said, making it easier to deploy in times of crisis.

“Central banks can more easily lend their gold there to other banking institutions.”

John Plassard, an analyst at Cite Gestion Private Bank, said the Dutch move was intended “for there to be more immediate availability in the event of a crisis”.

For the moment, it was a “fairly one-off move”, but he warned that if other central banks followed suit, it could damage confidence in the US.

At the beginning of the year, there were concerns raised in Germany about the security of its central bank’s reserves in New York.

However, the powerful Bundesbank has decided for the moment not to shift its reserves away from New York.

“The New York Fed is and remains an important storage site for our gold,” the bank told public TV station ARD in January.

stories.title: Almost half of households do not see benefits of economic growth, report says
stories.summary: Analysis has found a "stark" gap in the spending power of households in the north and south of England on average.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 3 September 2026, 00:26 BST

Almost half of people in Britain live in areas where economic growth does not translate into a better quality of life with a "stark" North-South divide in the spending power of households, a new report finds.

Researchers at consultancy PwC said every region in the north of England, Midlands and Wales had lower spending power than the country's average, with London and the South East comfortably above.

The findings come as Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to tackle regional inequalities in a bid to boost living standards across the country.

But questions remain over the PM's plans, with surging government borrowing costs set to limit his room for manoeuvre at October's Budget.

The PwC report said the equivalent of 12.5 million households - 46% - lived in parts of the country where economic growth, often seen through increased business investment and job opportunities, was not leading to better living standards.

It said households in the north east of England had 6.6% less spending power than the national average, equivalent to £1,542 less a year. The North West was £1,493 less, while Yorkshire and the Humber were worst off with spending power down £1,917 comparatively.

Meanwhile, households in the South East were found to have spending power 9% above the national average, worth an additional £2,154 a year, followed by London.

Household spending power is seen as a good measure of whether economic growth is improving living standards.

PwC says it measures this by looking at income after taxes and housing costs, and takes into account the size and makeup of a household - which is aimed at giving a better idea of the money available to meet other expenses.

The UK has seen years of slow growth, although the economy expanded by 1.2% in the first six months of this year, according to official figures.

Economic growth usually means people spend more, extra jobs are created, more tax is paid to the government and workers get paid better.

In theory, this leaves people better off. But it takes time for the benefits to be felt, and it does not necessarily benefit everyone. According to PwC, "only a fraction" of a rise in GDP - the size of the economy - leads to increased spending power.

Researchers said while there was a clear North-South divide in the spending power of households, there were also examples of spending power differences within areas deemed better off, such as London and the south east.

For example, Richmond's average annual disposable income was the highest in London at £35,448 - almost double the £18,384 recorded in neighbouring Hammersmith and Fulham.

"The research shows just how differently prosperity is experienced across the UK, with stark variations not only between regions but on each other's doorstep," said Rachel Taylor, government and health industries leader at PwC.

Though spending power in the south of England is impacted by higher housing costs compared to the north, the hit to households on average is softened by higher incomes and the divide remains, researchers said.

Scotland and the south west of England were exceptions to the trend, the report added, because lower housing costs and smaller households meant spending power was slightly above the national average.

The report argued that the next phase of transferring power from central government to local authorities - known as devolution - "must allow local areas to retain more of the revenues generated by local growth alongside more freedom on how best to use resources".

But it said success "should be judged not simply by whether local economies grow, but by whether that growth leads to greater prosperity, wider opportunity and better lives for the people and communities within them".

Devolution has been a central part of Burnham's leadership so far, including his pledge to create "the conditions for good growth in every postcode" .

A government spokesperson said the creation of No10 North was part of its growth mission and would reshape "how the country is run".

"We have already announced unprecedented financial powers to English mayors so they can receive a share of income tax revenues to boost local economies and improve public services," they added.

However, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said that Burnham's "diagnosis" and "theory of growth is completely wrong".

"He thinks that if government spends more money, we will all get richer - that is not how this works," she said. She has also called the establishment of No10 North a "gimmick".

stories.body:
For Andy Burnham, walking into the bear pit that is Prime Minister’s Questions, it must have been hard to stay calm. His audience was a room of closely packed MPs, some hostile, some friendly – all very loud – many wanting to make a mark.

And the full audience for PMQs extends far beyond the MPs in the chamber. Prime ministers are thinking about the media, external groups, foreign governments, voters and financial markets. The reactions of any of these matter. The PM has the dual worry of dealing with opposition questions while also demonstrating his or her worth to the party members sitting behind them. Backbenchers can signal a lack of confidence through quietness or just not turning up.

It is no wonder that preparing for PMQs is, in itself, demanding. Alastair Campbell, who advised Tony Blair when he was opposition leader and in the early days of the New Labour government, is clear about just what it took . Preparation can take hours. Nerves don’t disappear. And it doesn’t appear to have got any easier in recent years.

Burnham is, of course, new to this. And unlike many in his position, he hasn’t had a chance to rehearse as opposition leader. He was wise to spend part of Tuesday’s return to parliament on a statement and a lengthy question-and-answer session . It gave him a warm-up for the main event.

After Keir Starmer was ousted as prime minister, Labour MPs will be willing Burnham to show that he can succeed. So how did he do in his first PMQs, and what can we glean from it?

Restraint?

This was not a “full-blooded” PMQs. Burham chose not to mount attacks where others might have. A question from Reform UK’s Danny Kruger, for example, could have led to a reply focusing on the party’s reported problems . That it did not, may mean Burnham wants to move away from such attacks – or that he considers Reform less significant than it has been in recent years.

Burnham’s jibes at the Conservatives were not fierce either. He merely criticised past statements made by Tory leader Kemi Badenoch and her shadow cabinet and sought to associate them with the economic failings of past governments. Prime Minister’s Questions is an adversarial event and it will be worth watching whether more obvious hostilities develop in future.

Sharper exchanges in turn end up generating sharper questions, so PMQs could move from point-scoring debate to abusive exchange. But Burnham may have some way to go to match David Cameron, who was identified by researchers as the rudest prime minister at PMQs.

At length

Speaker Lindsay Hoyle warned that Burnham’s long answers may cause the session to overrun. Burnham clearly wanted to spend time on each answer, but this can be a blessing and a curse for a PM. Longer answers mean you can say everything you want. But sometimes the short, sharp reply is most effective at putting your opponent off their stride. The prime minister may have to learn brevity.

Moving on

One of the tricks of dealing with difficult subjects is the “bridge”. That is, taking the topic and linking to something else that you actually do want to talk about. Burnham showed some ability here, linking at one point from a question about public spending to the needs of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets).

His bridge from the Bayeux Tapestry and French president Emmanuel Macron to small boat crossings didn’t work, however. He is clearly a bit rusty in the use of this technique.

Are you listening?

Badenoch was keen to paint the PM as someone who won’t answer questions about spending, and as such as a PM who leans towards more tax and more spend. This may be the beginning of a strategy to frame him as vague and unwilling to commit to specific action in the face of obvious problems. Once an idea like this takes root, it is very hard to shift.

But neither Badenoch nor Burnham has the proper measure of the other yet, and it will take a few more outings before there is a sense of how successful this strategy may prove.

The right man for the job?

As Burnham did not ascend to Downing Street immediately after a run of other roles in parliament, or after a general election, he needed to make his experience clear. He name-checked things he had achieved or initiated, specifically in Greater Manchester, as a way of underlining his credentials.

These references, plus the use of “I”, were designed to demonstrate his ability to get things done, rather like the way it is used in job interviews. Using “I” instead of “my government” or “we” also demonstrates engagement with the topic .

Play nicely

During some replies, Burnham touched on cross-party working, and made an on-the-spot pledge to meet Cornish MPs (not all of whom are Labour) for talks. Offering cross-party working can remove the sting from an attack and make the prime minister seem reasonable. This appears to be a feature of Burnham’s approach and it will be interesting to see if it develops into genuine cooperation with at least some other parties.

Prime ministers often say they want to change aspects of PMQs. Burnham himself has indicated that he wants a different, less Punch-and-Judy tone. Back in 1997, Tony Blair made the move from two shorter sessions a week to one longer one . Blair said he wanted a more considered approach, with more questions and more answers. Whether prime ministers get what they want, of course, is not entirely down to them. They may get the last word, but they don’t control the cast.
